analysis.title: THINK Ahead: Markets get a fright, but central banks won't spook that easily
key_insights: Oil is down 14% since last week's close, natural gas down 16% and the Nasdaq down more than 6%. This is the backdrop for the Bank of England's first rate hike since the Iran war. Sweden, Australia and the Czech Republic also tightened.

Neither an ECB nor a Fed hike is fully priced for December. The probability of a Fed December hike has fallen to 70%. Rates priced one year ahead have dropped almost 50bp in both dollars and euros since late September.

ING thinks the market repricing is premature and that central bank pricing was already too aggressive. The author does not think the past week, including the US midterms, has changed the short-term policy outlook.

The energy price drop is not built on much. If diplomacy could not deliver a solution before the elections, it is unclear why it would now. Oil could fall further if the war does not escalate, since the commodities team sees the risk premium eroding. BoE Governor Bailey argued that what matters is what prices say about escalation risk, so central banks have reason to tread carefully if prices fall while geopolitics stay volatile.

Inflation is already embedded. Eurozone producer price inflation topped 11% in September. In the UK, energy is set to add more than one percentage point to inflation through next summer unless something changes dramatically.

There is no sign yet of energy costs spilling into the wider European inflation basket, and ING does not expect that at scale. The BoE is not reassured: it argues longer energy-price fixes than in 2022 may be delaying the hit to firms, and one-off employee bonus pressure has been lower than four years ago but could change as utility bills rise. Several more months of data are needed to calm concern about second-round effects.

In the US, core inflation remains too hot for the Fed. Six-month annualised rates of both main inflation measures are around 3%. Chair Warsh's preferred breadth gauge shows the share of categories above 3% inflation has fallen but remains high. In September, all but two Fed officials saw more rate hikes this year, so the bar to reverse is high.

Growth has been resilient. US investment tailwinds are unlikely to vanish immediately. In the UK, data centre investment and professional services output are likely to account for more than half of Q3 growth while being 14% of GDP. Tech is a large driver in the Netherlands, and German production rose solidly in the summer despite low water levels and higher energy prices.

Financial markets are the factor that could stop central banks in December. Warsh has rationalised a large part of the Fed's hikes through loose financial conditions, seen as a euphemism for high equity prices. A much deeper correction in AI stocks could raise doubts about a December Fed hike. Warsh sounded somewhat more cautious at the October meeting.
For the ECB, the French situation would need to get much messier to disrupt a December hike.

US outlook (James Knightley): at least eight Fed officials are scheduled to speak next week and are expected to be cautious. None are prepared to give a number for how many more hikes are needed. ING forecasts one December hike, citing a cooling housing market, weak wage growth and cautious optimism about a diplomatic solution to the Iran-US standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.

October CPI (Tuesday): ING expects headline and core to rise 0.3% month-on-month, above the 0.17% monthly pace needed to bring inflation to 2% year-on-year. Markets are likely to stay priced for a 25bp December FOMC hike. BLS will not publish year-on-year figures because October last year had a government shutdown with no data collected.

UK Q3 GDP (Thursday): monthly data for July and August already show a blockbuster quarter, partly from AI investment and a surge in services such as legal and advertising. ING is sceptical this is all AI productivity and sees a possible near-term pullback in monthly GDP, adding to the expected winter consumer slowdown.

sector_views.rationale: The sell-off in AI stocks matters for policy because Warsh has justified part of the hikes by loose financial conditions. A much deeper correction could raise doubts about a December Fed hike.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets are pricing a shorter hiking cycle. Oil is down 14%, natural gas down 16% and the Nasdaq down more than 6%. Neither an ECB nor a Fed December hike is fully priced, the Fed at 70%, and one-year-ahead rates are down almost 50bp.
tension_points.bear_case: ING argues central banks need more convincing. Core inflation is around 3% on a six-month annualised basis, Eurozone PPI topped 11%, growth has been resilient, and all but two Fed officials saw more hikes this year in September.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A much deeper correction in AI stocks that tightens financial conditions, or a messier French political situation for the ECB, could derail a December hike.

theme_stances.key_argument: Market pricing for fewer hikes is premature because inflation and growth data have not changed enough to stop central banks in December.
theme_stances.evidence: But even after a roller coaster week, central banks will take more convincing.
